## Design

### 2026-11-04: I worked on creating the BOM and solidifying the idea. I decided to do the BOM first because I wasn't sure that the components would fit under the 30$ limit of tier 1, which is what I am aiming for.

**2h**

I worked on creating the BOM and solidifying the idea. I decided to do the BOM first because I wasn't sure that the components would fit under the 30$ limit of tier 1, which is what I am aiming for.  I decided there's no need for a custom PCB because it would make things neater, but it's not really necessary, and I wanted to try something new because I have made 3 other PCBs for this Hack Club. I haven't really done direct soldering or soldering using a perfboard before, so it's good to learn. I did have to cut some sensors from my original idea to fall under the limit, but it's not exactly a bad thing, as I still have all the necessary components. I wanted it to be a standalone thing with a LiPo battery or something, but I realised it's better to make it wall-powered. Then, to save on cost, because I already have a USB-C breakout board, I decided to power it from USB-C, but it would just not provide as much power, so the LEDs can't be as bright, which is fine. It took me a really long time to find all the parts and "finalise," but I can still make changes ofc, to the parts list before I start making it. By the end of it, I got it under the 30$ limit.

### 2026-11-05: I worked on the schematic. I know that I am not using a custom PCB for this, but I decided to do the schematic, layout, and routing of the board so that when I actually make it, it is easy to see what

**3h**

I worked on the schematic. I know that I am not using a custom PCB for this, but I decided to do the schematic, layout, and routing of the board so that when I actually make it, it is easy to see what connects to what and where everything should be placed. I started by finding the footprints for things that were not already there on SnapEDA and then importing them. Then I started doing all the connections. I had to learn what each of the pins did, as I haven't used these components before, but it didn't take as long as I thought because I have used similar components, so I could figure it out faster. At first I didn't fully understand where each component connects, so the v1 of the schematic was wrong, slightly

And then after some changes I ran the ERC and I got a error because I didn't have a PWR_FLAG for the VBUS net, and I got some warnings about the power and gnd pins on the BH1750 being bidirectional and I am putting power there but its fine its not important.

### 2026-11-07: I did the layout and routing of the components. I know there is no actual PCB, but it just makes it much easier to visualize what is happening, what connects to what, and in what order. This way it wi

**2h**

I did the layout and routing of the components. I know there is no actual PCB, but it just makes it much easier to visualize what is happening, what connects to what, and in what order. This way it will make my life easy when I go to actually handwire things with stuff like perfboards or whatever, so much higher chance of nothing being wrong. I started with the RGB lights as that was the most important; I needed to know what the resistor connects to, what the capacitor connects to, what the level shifter connects to, etc. This is how it turned out:

![RGBStripIndividual](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/fa341c011d436719cfd5f2c9c1061ae9c2877349d575e74a78760a1abe630396.png)

Next, I did the power system, the next most important thing. I had to figure out where the fuse connects, where the usb c breakout board connects, where the screw terminals connect, etc. It actually was easier than I thought: the fuse connects to the screw terminal VBUS and 5V, the screw terminal connects to the GND and fuse, and the usb c breakout board connects to the GND and power of the screw terminal. This is what goes into the screw terminal from the top.

![PowerSystemIndividual](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/a524654e43a1bfba54987babfe90cfd1d28fa6e16a3aa9913423ddc6db26001c.png)

Then I did the BH1750 light sensor, initially I had the footprint as just connectors because I didn't think it mattered, but then it was making things more difficult to figure out and in general I wanted a cleaner, more concrete result. So I added the footprint library from SnapEDA and used that (like I was using for the symbol) which did need me to restart the routing and layout for that part but it wasn't too hard.

![BH1750Individual](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/d2d701973c88a891933852732f38fdf52ac3ec18f74091e96548c8730ceee93a.png)

Then the last component was the LD2410C motion sensor. I had the exact same issue with this one. I had it as a connector initially, but I didn't really know if I was doing it right, so I took the time to find the right footprint and used that. Also, for both of them, I realised I already had the footprint downloaded; I just didn't import it, which is why I couldn't use it. This took me a while to figure out, unfortunately.  Anyway, the wiring for the LD2410C was pretty easy.

![LD2410CIndividual](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/a67f4ea5040fb4c51431ddb07572d6e6f47cf5b28656f284231fe956b587b4dd.png)

Here is the finished layout and routing. The layout is not as important because everything will be hand-wired and soldered with no custom PCB, but I wanted the routing to make sure I know what connects to what exactly.

![FinishedRouting](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/9aeb6e9caf15b009d35c1d281e6644a4edcd9a4a96ef5edce0b18241b2e4098e.png)

![DRCNoErrors](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/1611f17f00f3c02a03de4e1598b1e4c7f0952f86193ecfa71a1afa01290e54c1.png)

### 2026-11-08: I made the CAD for the case that all the components will sit in. I wanted to make sure that each sensor has a specific slot to sit in, and that the USB-C for power and programming have holes, along wi

**3h**

I made the CAD for the case that all the components will sit in. I wanted to make sure that each sensor has a specific slot to sit in, and that the USB-C for power and programming have holes, along with a spot for the wires for the RGB to exit. The goal of the CAD was to be as parametric as possible, allowing for easy changes when the parts actually arrive so that I can edit the dimensions as I measure them and find the actual measurements.

I started with the base and main walls. I chose the dimensions based on approximation, allowing for more concrete measurements to be put in once the electronics arrive and the proper layout is confirmed in real life. I also added pillars for heat-set inserts to make it so I can screw the lid onto the main base.

![CADStartingSketch](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/75d828f1c77cd82a1cf1a0bb66060fef2b56cdf9d4a531eb4324353228bad9a7.png)

Then I made the holes for the light sensor and the motion sensor. For the light sensor, it was just a hole, and for the motion sensor, I exposed basically the whole sensor because I wasn't 100% sure which part of it was the actual sensor. I made it as relative to each other as possible, so changing just the dimensions of the holes to the actual sensor's dimensions should be enough to update everything else.

![CADSensorHoles](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/7ce3b27838f8c8a241e28923b8d965f50fc9f7ff53c0cc284362b27bc965f650.png)

Then I added sockets, where the sensors could slide into them to keep them upright and in the same position all the time. I really tried to make this as parametric as possible so that just changing the dimensions of the holes made earlier would adjust the sockets themselves, only needing the thickness of the sensor itself. This took a really long time to get right because stuff would randomly start warping. I also added a place for the usb c breakout board to sit so that it is stable if the board is ever moved around, making sure the usb c cord isn't ripped out or flung around inside.

![CADAddedSockets](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/b1a918bcf9e98fed4c987e44674838335707ccc63a46e9034730ec2d44abe8c5.png)

I then added the holes for the USB-C ports on the breakout board and the programming ports (there are 2). I also added a hole for the wires of the RGB light to go out of the box to connect to the RGB lights themselves. For the breakout board, I tried to make it based on the location of the breakout board socket, so that I only need to change the location of that to change the location of the hole. And the height of the usb c port from the bottom of the breakout board itself. For the holes for the programming USBs, I just guessed the location entirely, and will change it when the actual parts come in and are assembled. Same for the RGB light's wires.

![CADBaseDone](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/7ae3297137df0be9387738fe1e039d4dc9b229d2d29a2427ed59342fd1db15ad.png)

Then I went through and filleted most of the holes to make it look nice and easier to work with. I also did the edges and made the fillet have the same center as the pillars for the screws to make everything look cohesive and nice.

![CADBaseDoneFilleted](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/05db4d975e1dcdd7d6211de4fce6a3bbd542edd5ef474287681d737a7a277267.png)

Then I made the lid. I learnt how to make a part derived from another part. So I created a new parts studio, then I added a derive of the main object. Then I just made a sketch of the top and extruded it up 2 mm for the lid. This made it really nice so that if I change the size of the original base and stuff, it will update the size of the lid. This was a new learning for me and really cool because I wanted something as parametric as this. Overall, I am quite happy with how the CAD turned out.

![CADLid](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/61dfa92d98a100b8a88c47d0bd66f863f07ad9577cc3c05f5a89dff3af8779f4.png)
